newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb parliament seeks ouster of president. [CORRECTED 15:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb parliament seeks ouster of president. [CORRECTED 15:40 GMT]

text.p: Hardline nationalists ignored President Biljana Plavsic's order to disband the Bosnian Serb parliament and went ahead on Friday (corrects day from Thursday) with a session which will try to remove her from power.

Plavsic's dismissal was part of an agenda devoted to her conflict with the government and ex-president Radovan Karadzic, who was forced to resign from all public offices a year ago as an indictee of the U.N. war crimes tribunal.

Opposition and Moslem legislators stayed away from the parliament session in a ski resort hotel near the hardliners' stronghold of Pale, making it likely that Karadzic and his allies would get their way.

Any attempt to topple Plavsic would put the hardliners on a collision course with international mediators implementing the 1995 peace agreement. The mediators have endorsed her constitutional authority in the Serb Republic entity of Bosnia.

Plavsic, accusing the ultra-nationalists of corrupting the government and isolating Bosnian Serbs from the world by obstructing the implementation of peace measures, dissolved parliament on Thursday and set new elections for September 1.
She was supported on Friday by 7,000 demonstrators who gathered outside her office in the northern town of Banja Luka and urged her not to back down.
"I'm sorry this happened but crime must be stopped," Plavsic told them. "(War) victims did not fall for a state of thieves but for a state of honest people."

Representatives of the United Nations and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in Sarajevo warned the Serb hardliners that they would not recognise decisions taken by parliament now.

Simon Haselock, spokesman for the U.N. High Representative in Bosnia, told reporters: "Since the assembly has been dissolved, anything that meets this afternoon cannot be considered an assembly meeting.
"Clearly the international community will deal only with constitutionally recognised bodies. But we still have to see what happens in the next 24 hours. That will be crucial."

Western mediators did not hide that efforts to rebuild Bosnia based on the Dayton peace agreement, which set up a Serb Republic and Moslem-Croat Federation loosely linked by a multi-ethnic presidency, were at a turning point.

A diplomat in Sarajevo said: "If we are willing to see the one person in power in Republika Srpska (Serb Republic) who is willing to carry out the peace agreement be crushed by an indicted war criminal, where are we?"
Karadzic's chances of forcing parliament to do his bidding improved when the 14-strong bloc of legislators from the Moslem Party of Democratic Action (SDA) decided not to attend.
Without their votes, it was unlikely that members of the ruling Serb Democratic Party (SDS) who support Plavsic would be strong enough to prevent their foes getting their way.

By making public allegations of profiteering and smuggling against named government leaders and shedding light on Karadzic's illegal backroom influence, Plavsic has dealt the Bosnian Serb wartime elite a possibly crippling blow.

The feud has reinflamed antagonism between hardliners, based in the ski resort of Pale outside Sarajevo, and Plavsic's supporters in Banja Luka who believe Western peacemaking cannot be defied indefinitely.

Karadzic and close associate Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of the multi-ethnic presidency, were the two most powerful figures in the Bosnian Serb war to dismember Bosnia and have now been denounced by Plavsic for trying to enrich themselves by running monopolies dominating the economy.

Plavsic had no less a hardline reputation than Karadzic during the war but as postwar president appears to have come around to the need for mending relations with the international community to foster economic reconstruction in Serb territory.
Karadzic aide Jovan Zametica told reporters in Pale: "I am not ready to say that we have a constitutional crisis, but we definitely have a political crisis."
The independent Belgrade news agency Beta quoted Plavsic as saying she feared her life may be in danger over her revelations about corruption.
She alleged that three members of Bosnian Serb state security forces who were found in a room opposite her office on Thursday were monitoring her movements.
